item.title: Creativity and Curiosity Are Still Important in the Age of AI
item.description:
Creativity

Creativity and Curiosity Are Still Important in the Age of AI

Being willing to try new things makes us better problem-solvers and more resilient.

Posted July 21, 2026

Key points
  • Being creative and curious are soft skills that improve our ability to solve problems.
  • Both concepts are linked to greater joy in life and better stress tolerance, even among young people.
  • Creativity and curiosity help us find new solutions to problems.

There is a wonderful advertisement for Lee Valley Tools where they show nothing but a woodworker’s hands cutting and shaving wood, producing lots of sawdust and then scrap, as the piece of wood is thrown into a pile of waste. The narrator reminds us that it was all a great way to spend time, to learn new skills, to wile away the hours keeping busy and only sometimes ending up with anything to show for the time spent other than the satisfaction of the experience itself. Rather than focusing on success, the message is simple: the act of being creative is satisfying enough.

I’ve been wondering how our desire for output rather than quality is threatening our sense of meaning. What happens when fast fashion makes us feel momentarily trendy (with little effort or creativity)? Or when artificial intelligence provides us within seconds with the words for a speech at a friend’s wedding, a song, or a design to make our front yard look like the perfect holiday setting? What gets lost when creativity is removed from our lives? If we stop being curious and motivated to learn new things and even fail while learning, does that undermine our sense of self-efficacy and overall resilience to stress?

The woodworking advertisement gives me hope that there is still a desire to be creative. To embrace curiosity. A newly published study by Laura Cruz and her colleagues at Pennsylvania State University found that a positive attitude towards living life with curiosity is still very much valued. Cruz surveyed 650 undergraduate students, asking them about their level of motivation to learn new things. Overall, the results showed that most engaged in thinking creatively about solutions and were more than willing to tackle complex problems. From the perspective of building resilience, students who showed more curiosity tended to also score higher on questions that measured joy and stress tolerance. In other words, just like a home hobbyist wasting a Saturday afternoon accomplishing little but enjoying the time spent trying, undergrad students may still be inclined towards what has been termed “epistemic curiosity.” They want to learn new ideas that challenge them to see the world differently. Even in this age of easy-to-find solutions, there is still something very human about wanting to muddle through and solve a problem ourselves.

Creativity and curiosity needn’t be so academic, though. One can experience both through activities as basic as choosing colorful socks to playfully dress up a business wardrobe. Creativity is a superpower that helps us envision what is new and possible. It is a process that does not flinch from taking risks. In fact, as the American psychologist Robert Sternberg found when he looked at creativity as a force for change, highly creative people will redefine problems rather than choosing the most efficient solution to problems as they already exist. Resilience relies on this same willingness to look for better ways to solve everyday problems and make ourselves feel whole.

How to Cultivate Creativity and Curiosity

So, what does it take to be creative? How can we remain curious? It’s long been understood that creativity and its sibling curiosity require skills to explore the world (woodworking skills, reading skills, critical thinking, etc.), a willingness to consider all possibilities, and finally, the motivation to persist through the discomfort of failure. Little wonder that people who are comfortable with creativity tend to be better problem-solvers and more likely to feel optimistic about their future. Get stuck in a rut doing the same thing over and over again, and one can see how one can survive but seldom thrive.

There are plenty of ways to assess your own level of creativity. Here are a few questions to get you started.

  • When you are short on funds, are you still able to find something fun to do?
  • When you see other people experiencing a problem, do you help them find a solution that they like?
  • Do you enjoy learning new skills?
  • Do you enjoy teaching others new things?
  • Rather than being bored, do you find ways to entertain yourself that don’t involve time spent passively on a screen?
  • Can you draw a picture of something you’ve never actually seen based only on someone else’s description of it (the quality of the drawing is not the point)?
  • Are you okay with trying new ways to express yourself?

In general, the more of these questions you answered “Yes” to, the more creative and curious you are. It’s those traits that may be useful the next time the unexpected happens and a new solution is needed to a problem that’s been difficult to solve. Turning to AI might be a quick way to resolve the issue, but it may not be the most satisfying or one that improves your overall sense of wellbeing.

item.title: How to Listen and Speak to Symptoms in Psychotherapy
item.description:
Therapy

How to Listen and Speak to Symptoms in Psychotherapy

What can we learn from listening to and hearing what our symptoms have to say?

Posted July 21, 2026

Key points
  • Symptoms are not just something to suppress as quickly as possible.
  • There are various therapeutic techniques for listening to and dialoging with one's symptoms.
  • It takes courage, patience, humility, and receptivity to truly hear what our symptoms are trying to tell us.

This post is Part 4 of a series.

There are certain types of psychotherapy that, unlike cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) or dialectical behavior therapy (DBT), consider signs and symptoms to be a way of communicating with ourselves and others and, therefore, encourage patients to carefully listen to what such sometimes seemingly senseless phenomena might have to say about how we are really feeling and what we can do if we wish to feel better. Here are a few examples.

Gestalt therapy

Famed and flamboyant psychiatrist and Gestalt therapist Frederick "Fritz" Perls (1893-1970) considered symptoms to be the consequence of "unfinished business" (i.e., unexpressed, suppressed, or unresolved emotions or impulses of which we are unaware that manifest themselves in sundry symptoms and signs). His rather theatrical, dramatic, and existential approach to such affective or somatic symptoms might be to encourage the patient to become more keenly aware in the present moment of what and how they are physically and emotionally experiencing the symptom as it is happening right now—sometimes urging them to intentionally amplify or exaggerate the symptom—to help discover and disclose its significance by becoming more conscious of what kind of inner conflict or tension could be motivating or producing it.

Or he might have the person enter into a guided dialog in the here-and-now with the reified symptom by employing his classic "empty chair technique" in which the patient converses with their symptom as if it were an embodied entity seated in a nearby sofa or chair—and, in some cases, physically switching seats to alternately respond and speak as the symptom—to try to discern what it might want of them as well as how or why they might be subconsciously contributing to, perpetuating, or, in effect, unconsciously creating their symptom. In this sense, symptoms can be conceived of as indirect and sometimes symbolic communications to ourselves and others from ourselves that there is some psychological, existential, or spiritual problem or conundrum in dire need of our immediate attention. For Perls, the originator of Gestalt therapy, cultivating more awareness, consciousness, or what we today call "mindfulness" of our symptoms can be the key to receiving, comprehending, and benefiting from their covert wisdom.

Dr. Rollo May (circa 1977)
Source: Wikimedia Commons, public doman

Existential therapy

Existential analysis or existential therapy is rooted in the European existential philosophy of Kierkegaard, Nietzsche, Husserl, Heidegger, and Sartre among many others and was developed and popularized by iconoclastic clinicians like Ludwig Binswanger, Medard Boss, and here in America, Rollo May and Irvin Yalom.

Some existential therapists, who, like Perls, emphasize here-and-now awareness of one's psychological, emotional, and physical subjective experience of being, in practice take a similar approach, encouraging the client (and themselves) to be fully present, to listen intently and phenomenologically (i.e., without preconception, prejudice, or presumption), to what the person's symptoms might be trying to tell them—especially about their existential anxieties, frustrations, and "ultimate concerns," such as aloneness, alienation, freedom, meaninglessness, responsibility, guilt, suffering, and mortality, encouraging them to carefully listen to and confront these existential concerns directly and consciously rather than avoiding, denying, or suppressing them.

Indeed, for existential therapy, symptoms are generally considered indicative of some conscious or unconscious conflict or fear regarding these so-called "givens" of human existence (see Yalom, 1980; Diamond, 2022). Symptoms such as neurotic anxiety are considered to be the result of choosing to chronically deny, avoid, or repress what existential therapists see as "normal" or existential anxiety—particularly "death anxiety"—an unavoidable, vital, and essential aspect of the human condition which we must learn to accept, tolerate, value, utilize, and live with as constructively or creatively as we can.

The experience of anxiety, which is not necessarily a neurotic symptom but often simply part of being human, is a central concern for existential therapy, and closely associated with our existential freedom. According to existential philosopher Søren Kierkegaard, "anxiety is the dizziness of freedom." So it is crucial to listen carefully and unassumingly to one's anxiety, both normal and neurotic, and what it might have to say, for as Kierkegaard (1957) proclaims, anxiety, when properly related to, can at times be our "best teacher." There are certain times when anxiety serves as an alarm or warning to be heeded and others when it is not referring to an experience to be avoided or suppressed but courageously confronted and embraced. For instance, legendary existential psychotherapist Rollo May (1909-1994) held that when we feel anxious, the anxiety may be telling us that something new needs to happen in our life; we need to make some decision, create something, change something, assert ourselves, take some risk, or confront our fears, and sometimes signals the imminence and necessity of such anxiety—provoking life choices. So, there is much to learn from our anxiety if we are truly willing to listen.

In Part 5 of this series, we will be discussing additional methods for listening and speaking to our psychiatric signs and symptoms from Jungian analysis and my own existential depth psychology (EDP).

Part 1 of this series can be found here. Part 2 can be found here. Part 3 can be found here.

item.title: How to Manage Your Inner Posse of Lawyers When It Pipes Up
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

How to Manage Your Inner Posse of Lawyers When It Pipes Up

Personal Perspective: My inner lawyers are trying to keep me safe.

Posted July 21, 2026

Source: Ghavam Cheraghalli / Unsplash

I have a posse of—apparently—Ivy League-educated prosecutorial lawyers in my head sometimes. But I’ve noticed lately they don’t hold the same power they used to. I also have another voice that could be described as a trusted friend. Instead of telling me I’m worthless and incapable, like my lawyers do, the voice of my trusted friend listens and responds with gentle reality checks and measured encouragement.

I don’t think I’m alone. At least I hope I'm not. We all have an inner voice—except for those who have anendophasia—but that’s not the focus of this post.

Of course, when I refer to my lawyers, I’m referring to my negative self-talk. But how exciting—or accurate—is it to call it merely negative self-talk? That label doesn’t even come close to capturing the nasty, vicious things my lawyers bring forward as evidence. I could call them the I.B.S.C.—the Itty Bitty Sh*@#y Committee. But again, they don’t feel so teeny weeny when they're shouting from their bullhorn.

Their volume is in stark contrast to how my trusted friend works. She is mostly quiet—strategically so. She patiently listens to the reasons why I think the lawyers are right. Then, with a calm voice and balanced opinion, she offers observations and simple suggestions. No toxic positivity coming from a squad of inner cheerleaders. God bless their misguided exuberance.

I heard about the inner lawyer concept from somatic practitioner Sarah Baldwin. We each have inner self-protectors trying to prevent us from getting hurt. I now use it as a jumping-off point to understand what’s happening internally.

However, I could never understand how cruel comments, like those from my lawyers, could be a form of protection. But then I realized the job of these seasoned, highly trained lawyers isn’t to make me feel bad; it’s to keep me safe.

They use everything in their power—threats and criticism—to convince me to stay put and not take a risk my nervous system has learned long ago to interpret as dangerous. Even when, in the present, it isn't. Maybe it’s sending a sales email, delivering a new keynote, or writing a memoir—all of which I’m in the process of doing. On days when stress and lack of sleep have caught up with me, or an old wound has been triggered, my team of malicious lawyers might pop up and start haranguing me. Their tirades can be defeatist, threatening, critical, or catastrophizing.

But in all cases, one thing I know for sure: if I argue with them, I won’t win.

Instead, I get curious. Why have they shown up? What are they trying to protect me from? The more I understand, the more my nervous system calms and the quieter the lawyers become. That’s when my wise, trusted friend who has been listening throughout can finally make a difference.

It’s okay. Things are difficult right now. But you’ve gone through hard things before, and you’ve moved through them before. You’ll get through this. You might not feel it, but you are capable, strong, and you have the power to choose. What’s the next best step?

She doesn’t give me useless, saccharine statements: Don’t worry. Everything will be fine. Trust life. Why don’t you give yourself a break and watch some TV?

I’m not saying self-care doesn’t have its place. It does. I’m a big fan of binge-watching Little House on the Prairie like the next person, but not when the best option is action; even if that action is a small step. Because often tiny is big and slow is smart.

What to Do When Your Posse of Lawyers Pipe Up

  1. Don’t argue; get curious.
  2. Ask: What danger are your lawyers trying to protect you from?
  3. Observe what happens in your body.
  4. Listen for your trusted friend’s perspective.
  5. Choose one action inspired by your trusted friend—despite your lawyers.

For example:

Lawyers: You’re an irrelevant keynote speaker. Your material is so dated. You’re never going to get hired again.

Don’t argue.

Me: Well, that’s not true. I may be working less, but that doesn’t mean I’m irrelevant…

Instead, get curious.

Me: Hmmm, I wonder what they’re trying to protect me from? They probably want to keep me from getting rejected if I put myself out there by making sales calls or presenting new material. I can understand that.

My body starts to relax, and my lawyers begin to quiet, because I’ve listened.

Then my trusted friend comes online.

Trusted friend: I know being vulnerable is scary, and you might not get the answer you want. But you’ll survive if you get a “no.” And if you do, you can pivot and try something new.

When my attorneys start up, I don’t need a splashy rebuttal. I need a strategy—and momentum. My lawyers try to keep me frozen and immobilized, and sometimes they succeed. But more often than not, after I’ve gotten curious and listened to what’s underneath the rants, my trusted friend comes alongside me, holds my hand, and helps me choose the BAM (bare-assed minimum) next step.

It’s not trendy. It’s not glamorous. But it is effective. The lawyers don’t always shut up. Sometimes they keep jabbering while I connect with my trusted friend and take action anyway.
